say: Good morning, inquirers! Today you are decimal detectives. Decimals hide in prices, in masses, in race times. A tiny digit after the point can win or lose a race.
Our rule today: notice the place, test with a number line, explain why.
Draw a box, a decimal point, then two boxes (three empty boxes, with the point after the first). I will turn over a digit card. Write it in a box straight away. You cannot move it later!
Our target is 5. The number closest to 5 wins. Where would you put a 4? A 9? A 0?
You have the cards 2, 5, 8 and a decimal point. How many different numbers do you think you can make? Write your guess before you start.
stuck: Stuck: put the point after the first card. Now swap the digit cards around. Then move the point.
Not sure if you have them all: “How many numbers start with 2? With 5? With 8? Where can the point go?”
Finished early: which number is closest to 50? Which two numbers are closest to each other?

say: “Where is the arrow? Between 2.3 and 2.4. I zoom in. That gap is cut into 10 equal steps, so each step is one hundredth, 0.01. The arrow is 6 steps past 2.3, so it is 2.36.”
“Which is bigger, 4.37 or 4.307? I line up the points. Same ones, same tenths. Hundredths: 7 and 0. 7 hundredths is more, so 4.37 is bigger, even though 4.307 has more digits.”

“A number with 2 decimal places rounds to 3.8. I look at the number line. The halfway marks are 3.75 and 3.85. 3.75 rounds up to 3.8, so it is the smallest. 3.85 would round up to 3.9, so the largest is 3.84.”

do: Ask: “What is one small step worth on this number line? How do you know?”
Ask: “Line up the decimal points. Which place do you compare first?”
Ask: “Would this number round up or down? Where is the halfway mark?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Write each number in the place-value chart. Fill empty places with 0.”
Hint 2: “Count the steps between the two labelled marks. Divide the gap by the number of steps.”
Hint 3: “For bars: take away the extra part first, then share the rest equally.”

say: “Ben says 3.405 is bigger than 3.45 because 405 is bigger than 45. Who agrees? How can we check?”
ask: “Ben says 3.405 is bigger than 3.45 because 405 is bigger than 45. Who agrees? How can we check?”
Ben is wrong. Line up the points: 3.405 and 3.450. The ones and tenths are the same; 0 hundredths is less than 5 hundredths, so 3.405 < 3.45.

say: “Today you zoomed in on number lines, lined up the points, and worked rounding backwards. Detectives check every clue, and you did. Well done, inquirers!”

p4l5-title.note: Objective: Read decimals to 3 places on number lines, compare and order them by place value, round to the nearest whole number, 1 or 2 decimal places and work backwards from a rounded number (smallest and largest), and solve money and mass puzzles with bar models. Thinking strategies today: ZOOM IN (what is one step worth?), LINE UP THE POINTS, MAKE A LIST IN ORDER, DRAW A BAR MODEL. Materials: Digit cards 0 to 9 and a decimal point card for each child, a place-value chart (ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths), mini whiteboards, a metre ruler, play money. Online: children cut out paper digit cards and a paper decimal point before the lesson and move them on camera; the tutor marks the zoom-in number lines on the slides. Time plan (90 minutes in all; every part has a budget and there is a 2.5-minute standing buffer inside the page-2 block). Opening 0 to 1.5. Sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6.5 (puzzle 1 about 60 seconds, puzzle 2 about 90 seconds, then ONE check moment for both puzzles; answers ticked or said together on three; nothing held up to the camera, nobody marked). Warm-up game 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds), quick questions 8.5 to 11.5 (three questions). Explore 11.5 to 25 (the only breakout of the first half: about 60 seconds each way, closed by a 60-second timer; a Go further what-if is on the slide from the start; two debrief questions). Teaching 25 to 33 (click to reveal each step and answer; the one "your turn" slide is optional: skip it if you are behind). Brain break 33 to 36.5 (water and toilet first, then the game; clock check at the end of the break: if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item, never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back). Worksheet 36.5 to 79.5: page 1 (Start here, in pairs) 36.5 to 55, check together 55 to 57, short teaching before page 2 57 to 62, page 2 on your own 62 to 77.5 (the last 2.5 minutes are the standing buffer: if earlier parts ran long, spend the buffer first, then the choice questions, and never the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back), check together 77.5 to 79.5. Talk time 79.5 to 83 (one minute of pair talk, no breakout). Exit ticket 83 to 86.5. Looking back 86.5 to 90 (2 minutes of writing). After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation have no fixed time slot: any child may choose them at any time, or take them home. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and pairs are not split unless both children agree. Online: page 1 is pair work, so allow about 2 minutes to move into and out of breakout rooms (or run page 1 as a whole-group screen-share if there are only 8 children).

p4l5-check.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6.5 (5 minutes). SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Say: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, drawing is welcome and so is saying I do not know. Nobody is marked, and nobody's answer is shown to the group." Puzzle 1 is a TRY IT puzzle: any child can start it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 needs a little thinking. Give about 60 seconds for puzzle 1 and about 90 seconds for puzzle 2. Children show their answers PRIVATELY: written on their own paper and said together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Make ONE check for both puzzles, after puzzle 2: children say the answers together on three. Never use private chat or DMs. Never ask for boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, never read out whose answer is whose, and never say who got it right. Then click to show each answer and talk it through for everyone ("some of you tried ..."), naming no child. Nobody is called on by name, and passing is always fine. ANSWERS: 1) Ali has more. $0.80 (8 tenths) is more than $0.75 (7 tenths and 5 hundredths). 0.8 is the same as 0.80, and 0.80 is bigger than 0.75. 2) Any decimal from 3.401 to 3.499, for example 3.45. Write 3.4 as 3.40 and 3.5 as 3.50: 3.45 sits between them. A GOOD REASON: Line up the decimal points and compare place by place. Write extra zeros so every number has the same number of places. Use what you see only to plan your help. It does not decide who is on which page and it is not recorded as a mark. ON PAGE 1 (printed): "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Make the invitation to the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"), so nobody is singled out. Never message a child privately, never name a child, and never announce who is on which page. Everyone stays in the same room and every child turns to the page they choose. If a pair would be split, ask both children first; never leave a child alone on page 1 (join them to another pair or to yourself).

p4l5-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds: the Sneak-peek puzzles came first). Target 5. Children draw three empty boxes with a point after the first on a whiteboard. Shuffle digit cards 0 to 9 and turn over one at a time (online: read the digit aloud; nothing is held up to the camera). After EACH card, children write it in one empty box at once and cannot move it. After three cards, everyone reads their number aloud; the number closest to 5 wins (work out how far each is from 5). Play ONE round (target 5; stop at about 90 seconds). Click to show the thinking question. Talk: "A 4 or a 5 belongs in the ones box: 4.9 something or 5.0 something is close to 5. A 9 in the ones box is a disaster. A 9 in the hundredths box hardly matters: it is only 9 hundredths." Listen for children who say "the ones digit matters most, then the tenths". That is the key idea of today.

p4l5-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 11.5. Three questions, about 30 seconds each: read each aloud, write it, say the answer together on three, then click to show. No follow-up questions. 1) 7 hundredths. 2) Watch for 0.64: the 4 must be in the thousandths place, so the hundredths place needs a 0. 3) Many children say 0.75 because 75 > 8. Write 0.80 under 0.75: 8 tenths beats 7 tenths. Finish with the line: "0.8 is the same as 0.80. 0.80 is bigger than 0.75." It comes back in the teaching. The other two warm-up questions (round 4.68 to 1 decimal place; how much more than $3.05 is $5?) are in the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math.

p4l5-explore1.note: Minutes 11.5 to 21.5. Pairs work with digit cards 2, 5, 8 and a decimal point card (online: paper cards on camera). Ask them to predict first: how many numbers? Let them record numbers in any order at first. Ask "Where can the point go?" (after the first digit or after the second digit; not at the start or the end, because then it is not between two digits). Go further (on the slide), for any child who wants it: which number is closest to 50? (52.8, only 2.8 away; 58.2 is 8.2 away). GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of the explore, so nobody waits): What if the target is 50 instead of 5? Which number with these cards is closest to 50? Answer: 52.8 (2.8 away). The next closest, 58.2, is 8.2 away.

p4l5-explore2.note: Minutes 21.5 to 25. Stop the hands-on after about 6 minutes (or when the 60-second timer closes the rooms) and finish ordering here, in the debrief. Two debrief questions only. Write their numbers on the board in the order they say them, messy on purpose, then ask "Is anything missing? Is anything there twice?" Answers: 1) 12 numbers. The three digits can be arranged 6 ways (258, 285, 528, 582, 825, 852) and the point can go in 2 places: 2.58, 2.85, 5.28, 5.82, 8.25, 8.52, 25.8, 28.5, 52.8, 58.2, 82.5, 85.2. 2) Smallest 2.58, largest 85.2. The third question (closest to 5: 5.28, only 0.28 away) is not asked; it comes back in the teaching.

p4l5-teach1.note: Teach. Start with the top line: "How many steps from 2 to 3? Ten. So each step is one tenth, 0.1." Point along: 2.1, 2.2, 2.3. Then the zoom: "The gap from 2.3 to 2.4 is cut into ten tiny steps. Each one is a tenth of a tenth: one hundredth, 0.01." Click step 1, step 2, then the answer. Think-aloud: "The arrow is 6 tiny steps past 2.3. So it is 2.3 and 6 hundredths: 2.36." Ask: "Can we zoom in again, between 2.36 and 2.37?" (yes: 10 steps of 0.001; halfway is 2.365). Use a metre ruler too: 1 m = 100 cm, so 2.36 m is 2 m 36 cm.

p4l5-we1.note: Line up the points: today's main idea. Click to fill each row of the place-value chart; children say the digits first. Point out the 0s in grey places: "4.37 has no thousandths. I can write a 0 there: 4.370. It is the same number." Then the side notes. Think-aloud: "All have 4 ones. Tenths: 3, 3, 0, 3. The 0 tenths is smallest: 4.073. Now 4.300, 4.307, 4.370. Hundredths: 0, 0, 7. So 4.37 is the biggest. 4.300 and 4.307: thousandths 0 and 7, so 4.3 comes first." Common mistake: "4.307 has more digits so it is bigger." Show 4.307 and 4.37 on a zoom number line if needed.

p4l5-we2.note: Click through the steps. Think-aloud: "Rounding to 1 decimal place means: which tenth is it nearest to? 6.47 is between 6.4 and 6.5. The halfway mark is 6.45. 6.47 is past it, so 6.5." Then the whole number: "Which whole numbers is it between? 6 and 7. Halfway is 6.5, and 6.47 has not reached it, so it rounds to 6." Rule we use: exactly halfway rounds UP (6.45 rounds to 6.5). The two answers differ because we are looking for different neighbours.

p4l5-we3.note: This is the detective question: work backwards from the rounded number. Click to shade the band, then the steps. Before step 2 ask whether 3.85 is in or out. Many children say in. Test it: 3.85 is exactly halfway, so it rounds UP to 3.9. So the largest with 2 decimal places is 3.84. 3.75 to 3.84 are 10 numbers that round to 3.8.

p4l5-try2.note: Whiteboards. a) Neighbours 5.34 and 5.35, halfway 5.345; 5.349 is past it. b) Neighbours 12.9 and 13.0: write 13.0, not 13, to show 1 decimal place. c) Halfway marks 8.5 and 9.5. 8.50 rounds up to 9, so it is the smallest; 9.50 would round to 10, so the largest is 9.49.

p4l5-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Comparing decimals by the number of digits (3.405 > 3.45 because 405 > 45) instead of lining up the points. (2) Reading a number line by counting marks without first working out what one step is worth (0.1, 0.01 or 0.001). (3) Rounding backwards: giving 7.45 as the largest number that rounds to 7.4 (it rounds to 7.5), or forgetting 7.35 to 7.39, which are below 7.4.

p4l5-break.note: 3.5 minutes: water and toilet FIRST (about one minute), then the game (about two minutes), then back in your seats. CLOCK CHECK at the end of the break (minute 36.5): if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item (the "your turn" slide, a second speaker-note question), never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back. Call: 0.7, 0.45, 0.50, 0.09, 0.6, 0.555, 0.499, 0.5. Watch 0.45 (crouch, many stand) and 0.50 (freeze). Online: children stand and crouch in view of the camera.

p4l5-ws1.note: Minutes 36.5 to 55. Pairs do Q1 to Q3. Walk around. Ask "What is one step worth?" and "Which place do you compare first?" before giving any help. Q3 is part (a) only: the number line from 7.30 to 7.50 shows the halfway marks. How many numbers and the digit clue are in the question bank. CHOOSING (printed on page 1: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder."): invite the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"); never message a child privately, never name a child, never announce who is on which page. If one child of a pair wants to move on, do not split the pair unless both agree; if a pair does lose a member, join the other child to another pair or to yourself straight away. Children on Think harder keep working through the page check; reading along is optional.

p4l5-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1: line a steps are 0.1 (B is halfway between 6.8 and 6.9, so 6.85); line b steps are 0.01; line c steps are 0.001, so E is 0.247. f) only 6.85 rounds to 7. Q2b: line up the points: 3.405 and 3.450 have the same ones and tenths, but 0 hundredths is less than 5 hundredths. Q3: the halfway marks are 7.35 and 7.45; 7.45 rounds up to 7.5, so the largest is 7.44. (Question bank: 7.35 to 7.44 is 10 numbers, and the digits-adding-to-18 clue gives 7.38.)

p4l5-teachcards.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 uses digit cards 3, 6, 9). Ask first: "Which do you think is closer to 3?" Most children pick one side without checking. Click through. Think-aloud: "Below 3 I want the biggest number that starts with a smaller digit: 1, then the biggest digits: 1.84. Above 3 I want the smallest number starting with a bigger digit: 4.18. Now I measure both distances." The lesson: always check both sides of the target.

p4l5-teachbar.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). Draw the two bars first: "Who has more? Whose bar is longer? By how much?" Think-aloud: "If I cut off Ravi's extra 60 cents, the two bars are the same. Together they are $6.80 minus $0.60, which is $6.20. Shared equally: $6.20 divided by 2. 6 divided by 2 is 3, 20 cents divided by 2 is 10 cents: $3.10." Show the division as 6.20 ÷ 2 = 3.10 too. Always check BOTH clues at the end.

p4l5-teachmass.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6). Ask: "Why can't we just divide 2.3 by 5?" (the tray is on the scale too). Think-aloud: "First I take the tray away: 2.30 minus 0.55. I line up the points and write 2.3 as 2.30. That is 1.75 kg for 5 cups. Then 1.75 divided by 5: 175 hundredths divided by 5 is 35 hundredths, 0.35 kg." Q6b on the worksheet takes cans OUT: ask "How much mass leaves the scale?"

p4l5-teachclue.note: Optional stretch teaching (the mystery decimal with 3 places is Think harder Q4). Strategy: use the rounding clue to make a short list, then test every case against every clue. Ask after step 1: "Why only tenths 1 or 2?" (3.15 to 3.19 have tenths 1; 3.20 to 3.24 have tenths 2). Stress step 3: the case that breaks a clue must be crossed out out loud, so children see why the answer is the only one.

p4l5-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who still compare decimals by their number of digits. SOLO PAGE CAP: Page 2 is on your own. Aim for Q4 and Q5 first. Q6 is a choice for the last few minutes. Children who finish choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody is told which. BUFFER: the last 2.5 minutes of this block (minute 75 to 77.5) are the standing buffer. If earlier parts ran long, page 2 starts late and the buffer is spent first, then the choice questions at the end of the page. Never shorten the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back. Say nothing about the buffer to the children.

p4l5-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q4a: the decimal point goes after the first digit, so there are 6 numbers: 3.69, 3.96, 6.39, 6.93, 9.36, 9.63. Q4c: below 7 the best is 6.93 (0.07 away); above 7 it is 9.36 (2.36 away). Q4d: 3.69 and 3.96 both round to 4 (3.5 to 4.5). Q5: $9.40 − $1.20 = $8.20, $8.20 ÷ 2 = $4.10 for Siti, $4.10 + $1.20 = $5.30 for Mei. Q6: 2.85 − 0.45 = 2.40 kg for 6 cans, 2.40 ÷ 6 = 0.4 kg; 2 cans are 0.8 kg, 2.85 − 0.8 = 2.05 kg. (The mystery decimal 4.687 is Think harder Q4: it rounds to 4.7, so 4.650 to 4.749; tenths 6 gives hundredths 8, tenths 7 gives hundredths 9, which is too big; 4 + 6 + 8 = 18, so the thousandths digit is 7.)

p4l5-stretch.note: Answers (same four questions as the printed Think harder page): 1) 0, 1, 2 and 3 (3.45 is more than 3.42) 2) Smallest 9.50, largest 10.49 3) 2.65 and 2.605 4) 4.687 (rounds to 4.7, so tenths 6 or 7; tenths 7 would make hundredths 9, 4.79…, too big; so 4.68_ and 4 + 6 + 8 + 7 = 25).

p4l5-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) 2.459 (it is from 2.455 to 2.464; 2 + 4 + 5 + 9 = 20; 2.46_ would need an 8, but 2.468 rounds to 2.47). 2) 0.2 kg (the extra 2 apples weigh 0.95 − 0.45 = 0.5 kg, so 1 apple is 0.25 kg and the pear is 0.45 − 0.25 = 0.2 kg). More are in the question bank and on the Think harder pages.

p4l5-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: Q1, where do the numbers that round to 2.46 start and stop? Which tenths and hundredths digits can they have? Q2, what is the same in both bars? What is different? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p4l5-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: the rounding clue makes a short list (only 10 numbers), so we test cases instead of guessing. The second case is the trap: 2.468 has the right digit total but rounds to 2.47. Q2: lining up the two bars shows the extra 2 apples; this "compare and take away" idea is the same as the bar models on page 2.

p4l5-talk.note: Minutes 79.5 to 83. Pair talk is 1 minute (no breakout rooms: children tell the grown-up beside them, or write one sentence), then share. Answer: Ben is wrong. Line up the points: 3.405 and 3.450. Same ones, same tenths; 0 hundredths is less than 5 hundredths, so 3.405 is smaller. A number line check: 3.405 is just past 3.40; 3.45 is halfway to 3.5. Not asked in class (moved to the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math): "Why does 3.45 = 3.450, but 3.45 is not the same as 3.045?" (a 0 at the end adds nothing; a 0 after the point moves the other digits to smaller places). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a child may always pass; never call on a child by name to answer; no public tallies, scores or rankings; praise the reason, not the child. If a question uses a mistaken idea (a character who gets it wrong), present it as the character's idea and ask "What would you say to them?" so no child owns the mistake.

p4l5-exit.note: Minutes 83 to 86.5. Answer: 2.08, 2.088, 2.8 (as 2.080, 2.088, 2.800). 2.088 rounds to 2.1 (neighbours 2.0 and 2.1, halfway 2.05). Extension: use the digit cards 1, 3, 5, 7 and a decimal point to make the number with 2 decimal places that is closest to 40 (37.51).

p4l5-reflect.note: Minutes 86.5 to 90 (2 minutes of writing, 3.5 minutes with the routine). LOOKING BACK. Children fill in the box on the Investigation page, the page every child has (something I did well; the hardest part was; what helped me; one thing I could try next). Say one sentence: "Turn to page 3, the Looking back box. Write, tick or pass. Two minutes, no talking." The printed box says the rest. Model one yourself first: "Something I did well: I wrote the extra zeros. The hardest part was comparing decimals with different numbers of digits. What helped me: adding zeros so they had the same length. One thing I could try next: writing the zeros in a place-value chart." Say: "Ticking I am still stuck is a good thing to do: it tells me where to help." Do not ask anyone to read theirs out. If a child wants to share, take one volunteer and thank them for the strategy. Never grade it, never correct it, never collect it for marks and never show it to the group. Never ask a child to hold a page to the camera. Never ask for photos or private messages. If I am still stuck is ticked, check in during the open session: a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby. Never send a DM. Praise strategies ("you drew it", "you asked for help"), not speed or scores.
